subtitle: Present Simple · Tenses · Articles · Quantifiers · Numbers · Prepositions

blocks.narration: Welcome to the complete video guide to English for Engineering One, weeks one to four. In the next half hour we walk through every grammar rule, every question form and every answer pattern you need for Test One: the present simple and frequency adverbs, the tense contrast, the article system, quantifiers, the language of numbers, and the prepositions of movement and change. By the end, you will build correct English sentences and justify every choice you make. Let's begin.

blocks.title: The Course at a Glance
blocks.subtitle: What Test One is and what it rewards
blocks.narration: Chapter one. Before we touch the grammar, let's look at the map. This is a four-credit foundation course at Tashkent University of Technology: sixty classroom hours plus sixty hours of independent study. Test One is a paper-based writing task, one hour, ten percent of your grade. So every answer must be a complete, justified sentence.

blocks.heading: What This Course Trains
bullets: From school English to academic English
Core grammar: tenses, articles, quantifiers
Tasks: introductions, routines, definitions
Goal: follow engineering coursework in English
blocks.narration: What does this course actually train? The module description is clear: it moves you from general school English to confident, accurate, organized everyday and academic communication. The grammar core reviews the present simple, past simple, present perfect, quantifiers and relative clauses. The tasks are real communicative ones: introducing yourself, describing routines and past events, writing simple definitions. And the goal matters to every engineer watching: by the end you should have the English proficiency and academic communication skills needed to follow your engineering coursework in English. That is the finish line.

blocks.heading: The Road Through Weeks One to Four
bullets: Week 1: introductions; present simple
Week 2: tense contrast; articles
Week 3: numbers and quantifiers
Week 4: movement, prepositions; Test 1
blocks.narration: Here is the road map. Week one opens the course: you introduce yourself, your studies and your interests, and the grammar block is the present simple with adverbs of frequency. Week two works on semester planning: opinion language, generalizations, the tense contrast with the present continuous, and the article system. Week three is numbers and everyday quantification: quantifiers, proportions, averages. Week four turns to reading and writing about movement and change, with prepositions, and it closes with Test One on the week one to three material. Keep this map in mind; this video follows it.

blocks.heading: Assessment: Five Graded Components
blocks.narration: Now the numbers that decide your grade. The syllabus defines five graded components. Test One and Test Two are paper-based writing tasks, one hour each, worth ten percent each. Quizzes are written too: twenty minutes each, twenty percent together. The midterm adds reading and writing for thirty percent; the final brings reading, writing and listening for the remaining thirty. The grading scale: ninety to one hundred points is an A; seventy-five, a B; sixty, a C. And attendance matters: you must attend at least seventy-five percent of classes to sit the final exam.

blocks.heading: How to Answer in Writing
bullets: Write complete sentences, not notes
Choose the form, then justify the choice
Answer keys model sentences with reasons
Save 5 minutes to check verbs and articles
blocks.narration: Here is the single most important exam habit. The tests are writing tasks, so the answer keys in your study guide always model full written sentences: a correct form plus a short reason. When you choose a tense, justify it. Routine or permanent means present simple; happening now or temporary means present continuous; stative meaning forces the simple even for the present moment. Articles and quantifiers follow the same discipline. Then save the last five minutes to check verbs and articles — the checklist says most marks are lost there, not in ideas.

blocks.heading: Example: A Model Written Answer
blocks.problem: Opinion question: Have you ever felt that someone stereotyped you? How did you react?

steps.text: Plan: a personal story, then support
Story in past simple: Last year I assumed my classmate was unfriendly.
He never spoke — in fact he was simply shy.
Conclusion: present simple + frequency adverb
Now I try not to judge people before I talk to them properly.

blocks.result: A full answer: story, detail, conclusion
blocks.narration: Let's watch a strong written answer take shape. The question comes from the Week One listening task on stereotypes: have you ever felt stereotyped? How did you react? The advice: answer with a personal story, supported in two or three sentences. Step one, the plan: story first, then support. Step two, the story goes in past simple: last year I assumed my new classmate was unfriendly. Step three, the detail: he never spoke — in fact he was simply shy. Step four, the conclusion switches to present simple with a frequency adverb. Step five, the closing line: now I try not to judge people before I talk to them properly. Story, detail, conclusion — a complete, justified answer.

items: Test 1: paper-based writing, 1 hour, 10%
Course: 4 ECTS, 60 + 60 hours
Attend 75% of classes to sit the final
Write full sentences and justify them
blocks.narration: Chapter one in five lines. Test One is a paper-based writing task: one hour, ten percent. The course carries four credits, sixty classroom hours plus sixty hours of independent study. The grading scale runs from A at ninety points down to C at sixty. Seventy-five percent attendance is the minimum for the final exam. And the golden habit: write full sentences and justify the form you choose.

chapters.title: Week 1 — The Present Simple and Frequency

blocks.title: The Present Simple and Frequency
blocks.subtitle: Week 1: routines, habits, and how often
blocks.narration: Chapter two: week one, introductions. Students introduce themselves, their studies and their interests, and the first grammar block is the present simple with adverbs and expressions of frequency. Two questions drive this chapter: how do we talk about routines, and where exactly does the word for how often go in the sentence? Master these, and every getting-to-know-you conversation becomes easy.

blocks.heading: When We Use the Present Simple
bullets: Habits and routines: I play tennis every week
Always true: Sleep is really important
What we do every day, week or year
Generally true or always happens
blocks.narration: When do we use the present simple? Two big jobs. First, habits and routines: I play tennis every week. Second, things that are always true: sleep is really important for health. The lecture deck adds: things we do every day, every week or every year, or which are generally true or always happen. Notice what these share: none of them is about this exact moment. The present simple is the tense of general time — repeated actions and permanent facts. That is why its signal words are always, usually, often, sometimes, rarely and never.

blocks.heading: Present Simple: The Three Forms
blocks.narration: Form matters as much as meaning, so here is the form table. We build the present simple from the infinitive. With I, you, we and they, the affirmative is plain: I eat. The negative adds don't — you don't eat — and questions add do: do you eat? With he, she and it, the verb takes -s: she eats. The negative uses doesn't — he doesn't eat — and questions use does: does he eat? And the verb be is the rebel: I'm fit, they aren't fit, are you fit, she's fit, she isn't fit. No do and no does, ever.

blocks.heading: Spelling the Third Person -s
bullets: Most verbs: add -s — work, works
Consonant + y: -ies — study, studies
After sh, ch, ss, x: -es — finish, finishes
go, do add -es; have becomes has
blocks.narration: The third person -s has its own spelling rules, and Test One loves them. Most verbs simply add -s: work becomes works. A consonant plus y changes to i-e-s: study becomes studies. Verbs ending in the sounds s-h, c-h, double s or x take -e-s: finish becomes finishes. Two small verbs add -e-s too: go becomes goes, and do becomes does. And one true irregular: have becomes has. Say them aloud as you write. Five patterns — work, study, finish, go, have. Learn the labels; the answer key cites them beside every solution.

blocks.heading: The Frequency Scale
bullets: always, usually, often, sometimes
not often, rarely, hardly ever, never
The scale runs 100% down to 0%
I'm often late; We never eat out.
blocks.narration: How often? English answers with a scale that runs from one hundred percent down to zero. Always is every time; usually is most of the time; often and sometimes sit in the middle; not often, rarely and hardly ever push toward the bottom; never closes the scale at zero. Listen to them in real sentences: Mike usually goes for a run in the evening. I'm often late for work. We never eat out. Whole phrases work the same way: a hot drink five or six times a day; on holiday two or three times a year.

blocks.heading: Where Frequency Words Go
rows: She's always out at the weekend.
We don't often talk about politics.
I go to the gym twice a week.
blocks.narration: Position is where most marks are lost. Adverbs of frequency go before the main verb: they never eat out. But after the verb be: she's always out at the weekend. With don't or doesn't, the adverb still comes before the main verb: we don't often talk about politics. Two warnings: say she's never ill, never she's ill never; and with a positive verb use never — it never rains, never it doesn't never rain. Longer expressions like once a week normally go at the beginning or the end of the sentence: I go to the gym twice a week.

blocks.heading: Example: Building Questions
blocks.problem: Getting to know you: complete each question with a verb.

steps.text: Question word first: What languages?
Add do + subject: What languages do you?
Infinitive at the end: What languages do you speak?
Same engine: Where do you live? Do you have any pets?
What time do you usually go to bed?

blocks.narration: Time to build questions ourselves. The Week One poster asks eighteen getting-to-know-you questions, and every one runs on the same engine. Take the family block: what languages do you speak? Step one, start with the question word, what. Step two, add do plus the subject: what languages do you. Step three, finish with the infinitive: speak. Now watch the same engine drive the rest: where do you live? Do you have any brothers or sisters? With a frequency adverb: what time do you usually go to bed? And in the pair work, remember the strategy: answer, then return the question — and you, or what about you?

blocks.heading: Example: Word Order
blocks.problem: Put the words in the correct order: always before go I bed 11.00 to

steps.text: Find the subject: I
Adverb before the main verb: I always go
I always go to bed before 11.00.
After be: Laila is often late for work.
Kate hardly ever sees her family.

blocks.result: I always go to bed before 11.00.
blocks.narration: Second exercise: scrambled words, and the frequency rules put them back in order. The words are: always, before, go, I, bed, eleven o'clock, to. Step one, find the subject, I. Step two, apply the rule: the adverb goes before the main verb, so I always go. Step three, complete the tail: I always go to bed before eleven. Two variations from the same set. With the verb be, the adverb jumps after it: Laila is often late for work. And hardly ever behaves like a single frequency adverb: Kate hardly ever sees her family. And I visit my mum once a month — the expression sits at the end.

items: Present simple = routines + general truths
he/she/it adds -s; have becomes has
Negatives and questions: do / does + infinitive
Adverbs: before main verb, after be
Expressions: beginning or end of sentence
blocks.narration: Week one, compressed. The present simple covers routines and things that are always true. He, she and it add -s, and have becomes has. Negatives use don't or doesn't plus the infinitive; questions use do or does. Frequency adverbs sit before the main verb but after be. Long frequency expressions go at the beginning or end of the sentence. And keep conversations alive: return questions with and you?

chapters.title: Week 2 — Present Simple vs Present Continuous

blocks.title: Present Simple vs Present Continuous
blocks.subtitle: Week 2: general time or right now?
blocks.narration: Chapter three: week two brings the first big contrast, present simple versus present continuous. The tense review gives each tense a time idea, an auxiliary and signal words, and the Business Grammar book sharpens it into five semantic pairs. One question decides everything: is this general and permanent, or happening right now and temporary? And we will meet the classic trap, stative verbs.

blocks.heading: Present Simple: General Time
bullets: Time idea: GENERAL
Auxiliary: do / does
Signals: never, rarely, often, usually, always
Water boils at 100°C; She works in London
blocks.narration: Put the present simple under the microscope. Its time idea is general. Its auxiliary is do or does. Its signal words are the frequency family: never, rarely, hardly ever, sometimes, often, usually, always. Its two great uses: general truths — water boils at one hundred degrees; she works in London — and habits and regular occurrences — they go to Florida every summer. When you meet a frequency adverb or a phrase like every summer, your hand should already be writing the present simple. The tense review card prints these facts — memorize the card.

blocks.heading: Present Continuous: Now
bullets: Time idea: NOW
Auxiliary: be + verb + -ing
Signals: now, at the moment, these days
He is listening to the radio.
blocks.narration: Now its rival. The present continuous carries the time idea now. Its engine is the verb be plus the -ing form: am working, are working, is working. Its signal words are now, at the moment, at present, currently, these days. It describes actions that last over time and actions in progress — he is listening to the radio — and it can even carry insistence or emotion: I am telling you that it doesn't matter. When a sentence points at this moment, or at a temporary period around it, the continuous takes over.

blocks.heading: Five Pairs That Decide the Tense
rows: We are setting up a website.
blocks.narration: The Business Grammar pages organize the contrast into five examinable pairs; four sit in this table. Pair one, routine versus moment of speaking: we always collect the milk ourselves, but the production line isn't working at the moment. Pair two, general activities versus current projects: we design websites, and at the moment we are setting up a website for an agency. Pair three, permanent versus temporary: he still works for us; I am dealing with his clients this week. Pair four, facts versus slow changes: share prices vary, but the government is losing popularity right now. Same verb, different time idea, different tense.

blocks.heading: Stative Verbs: The Classic Trap
bullets: Thinking: think, know, mean, depend
Feeling + senses: want, like, sound, taste
Possession verbs are states too
I think we ought to give him the job.
blocks.narration: Now the trap Test One sets almost every year: stative verbs. Verbs of thinking — think, know, mean, depend — verbs of feeling and senses — want, like, sound, taste — and verbs of possession normally live in the present simple, even when we talk about now. I think we ought to give the job to Mr Janousek. What does this word mean? It all depends. But watch the twist: the same verb in its action meaning takes the continuous — we are interviewing people; I am trying to translate this letter. State, simple; activity, continuous.

blocks.heading: Example: The Dairy Interview
blocks.problem: Interview at a dairy: (the farmers / bring) it here themselves?

steps.text: you / usually organize the delivery — routine
Do you usually organize the delivery of milk?
the farmers / bring — routine: Do the farmers bring it?
we / always collect: We always collect the milk ourselves.
not work / at the moment: The line isn't working.

blocks.result: Routine takes the simple; at the moment takes the continuous
blocks.narration: Let's step inside a real exercise: an interview with Bill Cogges in the dairy business. Item one: do you usually organize the milk delivery to the factory? The word usually shouts routine, so present simple. Item two: do the farmers bring it here themselves? Same routine: do the farmers bring. Item three: we always collect the milk ourselves — the adverb always sits before collect, and the tankers deliver it to the plant twice a day. Then the mood changes. The production line isn't working at the moment — that phrase forces the continuous, because the employees are changing shifts. The procedure: find the signal word, ask routine or now, then commit.

blocks.heading: Example: Stative Verbs in Pairs
blocks.problem: We (interview) people for the new post, but I (think) we ought to give the job to Mr Janousek.

steps.text: interview — action in progress: are interviewing
think — an opinion, a state: I think
We are interviewing people, but I think we ought to give him the job.
survey now: are carrying out; customers: want
I am trying to translate; what does this word mean?

blocks.result: Action takes -ing; the state stays simple
blocks.narration: Exercise five is the stative-verb workout: each sentence holds one action verb and one state. The example: we are interviewing people for the new post — the action is in progress, so continuous — but I think we ought to give the job to Mr Janousek — think is an opinion, a state, so simple. Next: at the moment we are carrying out a survey to find out what after-sales service our customers want — want is a state. And the last one: I am trying to translate this letter and I don't know what this word means. Trying takes -ing; know and mean stay simple. The classic Test One trap — it cannot surprise you now.

items: General / permanent: present simple
Now / temporary / changing: continuous
usually, as a rule vs at the moment, these days
Stative verbs stay simple, even for now
blocks.narration: Week two, first half, in four lines. General, permanent or routine — present simple. Happening now, temporary, or slowly changing — present continuous. The signal words tell you which: usually and as a rule point to the simple; at the moment and these days point to the continuous. And stative verbs — think, know, want, mean — stay in the simple, even when you mean right now.

blocks.title: The Article System
blocks.subtitle: Week 2: a / an, the, or no article
blocks.narration: Chapter four: the second week-two grammar block, the article system. For every noun, English offers three choices: a or an, the, or no article at all. The test question is always the same: is this the first time we mention it, do we both know which one it is, or are we speaking in general? We will practice on real quotes about education.

blocks.heading: a / an — the Indefinite Article
bullets: First mention: Suddenly a man appeared.
What something is: She's a teacher.
An example: A thermometer measures temperature
Rates: 50 km an hour; 500 euros a month
blocks.narration: First, the indefinite article a and an. Use it when you first describe something, or make a general statement about something not known: suddenly a man appeared; that is an interesting point. Use it to say what something is or what somebody does: Paula is an Italian, she's a teacher, it's a racing bike. Use it to give an example: a thermometer is used for measuring temperature. And use it for rates and speeds: fifty kilometers an hour; five hundred euros a month. One spelling rule: an when the next word begins with a vowel sound.

blocks.heading: the — the Definite Article
bullets: Already mentioned: a dog; the dog
Made definite by details that follow
Known to both: the post office; the salt
Only one: The moon goes round the Earth.
blocks.narration: Second, the definite article the. Use it for things or people already mentioned: first I take a test tube, then into the test tube I pour fifty cubic centimeters of water. Use it when a noun is made definite by the details that follow: the man that the police were looking for. Use it when both speakers know what is meant: are you going to the post office? Pass me the salt. And when there is only one of something — the moon goes round the Earth — plus town places like the cinema, and superlatives: the best restaurant in town.

blocks.heading: Zero Article — Saying Nothing
bullets: General: Love makes the world go round.
General plurals: Doctors work 100+ hours
at / to / from + home, work, school
Meals, days, next/last: breakfast; next Friday
blocks.narration: Third, the zero article — the invisible one. Use no article for something general or uncountable: love makes the world go round; water boils at one hundred degrees. Use it with general examples: doctors often work more than a hundred hours a week. Use it with home, work, school and church after at, to and from: she's not at home today; I got to school late. Use it before meals, days and months — I never have breakfast — and with next and last: see you next week. But compare: I love flowers, general, with I love the flowers in my garden, specific.

blocks.heading: One Sentence, Three Choices
rows: I saw an old man with a dog.
the best cook in the world
blocks.narration: Watch the three articles fight over one idea. I saw an old man with a dog — both new, both take a. The dog was barking — second mention, we know which dog: the. I love flowers — general plural, no article. But the flowers in my garden — the clause defines them, so the returns. He's the best cook in the world — superlatives take the. And the frequency rate: we go to the theatre about once a month — a month, because frequency expressions use a with a singular noun. First mention, known, or general — that is the decision.

blocks.heading: Opinion and Generalizing Language
bullets: Opinions: should / shouldn't + verb
Personally, I don't think people should
In my opinion, e-scooters are dangerous
On the whole, they tend to spend time alone
blocks.narration: Week two also trains the language around the grammar. For opinions, use should or shouldn't with a verb: personally, I don't think people should need a driving licence; in my opinion, e-scooters are dangerous; but I think people should have to pass a test. For generalizations, five phrases to memorize: generally speaking, I think it's true that; in general, they behave in a more grown-up way; on the whole, only children are more independent; they tend to spend a lot of time by themselves; and they aren't always very good at sharing. Opinions with should, generalizations with tend to.

blocks.heading: Example: Quotes about Education
blocks.problem: Complete the quote: ___ child educated only at ___ school is ___ uneducated child.

steps.text: First mention: a child
school as an institution: at school — no article
an + vowel sound: an uneducated child
A child educated only at school is an uneducated child.
The greatest university of all is a collection of books.

blocks.result: a child; at school; an uneducated child
blocks.narration: Now the quotes exercise — five quotes about education, each a mini article test. Quote one, George Santayana: a child educated only at school is an uneducated child. Why? Child is a first mention, so a. School is uncountable in the fixed phrase at school, so no article. And uneducated begins with a vowel sound, so an. Quote two, Thomas Carlyle: the greatest university of all is a collection of books. Greatest is a superlative — the. Collection is a first mention — a. Books is a general plural — nothing. Quote three, Malala Yousafzai: extremists have shown what frightens them most — a girl with a book. General plural, then two first mentions. Five sentences, and every choice has a reason.

blocks.heading: Example: Articles in Dialogue
blocks.problem: Complete the dialogue: How often do you go to ___ gym? — About three times ___ week.

steps.text: the gym — a specific place we both know
a week — frequency: a + singular noun
What an amazing dress! — exclamation + vowel
I bought it in the sales last month.
a problem — then we solved the problem.

blocks.result: the gym; a week; an amazing dress
blocks.narration: The second exercise is a chain of mini-dialogues. Dialogue one: how often do you go to the gym? The gym is a specific place we both know — the. About three times a week — frequency expressions take a plus a singular noun. Dialogue three: what an amazing dress — exclamations with what take a or an, and amazing starts with a vowel sound. I bought it in the sales — a specific event — last month, no article before last plus a time word. The last dialogue shows the whole system in two lines: have you ever had a problem? First mention, a. Yes, but we solved the problem and got married. Second mention, the.

items: a/an: first mention, class, profession, rate
the: known, unique, superlative, town places
Zero: general plural, uncountable, meals
Opinions: should + verb
Generalizing: on the whole, tend to
blocks.narration: The article system in five lines. A or an for first mentions, classes, professions, rates and exclamations. The for things we both know, unique things, superlatives and places in town. Zero article for general plurals, uncountable ideas, meals and phrases like at home. Around it, the week's functional language: opinions with should, generalizations with generally speaking, on the whole, and tend to. Say the reason, not just the answer — that is what the test rewards.

blocks.title: Quantifiers
blocks.subtitle: Week 3: how much, how many, how little
blocks.narration: Chapter five: week three is all about quantity. The grammar block teaches quantifiers — much, many, few, little, enough — plus none, all, each, every, both, either and neither. The lecture adds the language of numbers itself. And the decision that drives the whole chapter comes before anything else: is the noun countable or uncountable?

blocks.heading: much, many, few, little — the Core Table
rows: We saw a lot of animals.
blocks.narration: Here is the core quantifier table, tested on tiger sentences. How many asks about countable nouns: how many tigers are there today? How much asks about mass: how much water on Earth? Not many and not much make negative statements: there aren't many tigers left; there isn't much time. A few and a little are positive: we managed to see a few tigers; there is a little water left. Few and little, without a, are negative in spirit — almost none: few conservationists believe tigers have a future. A lot of and lots of cover large quantities; too many and too much mean more than necessary: too many tourists, too much sunlight.

blocks.heading: Large, Small and Zero Quantities
bullets: Large: a lot of, lots of, loads of
a lot with no noun: James eats a lot
too big (never too much big); old enough
Zero: any + not; no + affirmative verb
blocks.narration: The lecture panel sorts quantity by size. Large: a lot of and lots of in affirmative sentences — my daughter has a lot of apps — and loads of is more informal. With no noun, drop the of: James eats a lot. Small: a little and a few mean some; very little and very few mean not much or not many. Two order traps: too big, never too much big — too much never precedes an adjective; and old enough, never enough old — enough follows the adjective. And zero quantity has two shapes: any with a negative verb, or no with an affirmative verb — there isn't any milk; there's no milk. In short answers: none.

blocks.heading: none, all, each, every
bullets: no + noun: No animal lives without water
none of: None of the students had done it
all (of) + plural: All animals need water
each test tube; every person (singular)
blocks.narration: Now the precise quantity words. No plus a noun describes zero: no animal lives long without water. None of means not one of a group: none of the students had done the work — and it takes a singular verb. All, with or without of, takes a plural noun and verb: all animals need water; you are all wrong after be; you have all made mistakes. Most means nearly all: most mammals have hair. Each looks at separate members — fifty cubic centimeters in each test tube — while every gathers the group: every person in the class took part. Each and every both take singular nouns.

blocks.heading: both, either, neither
bullets: Both books were written in 1985.
either = this one or the other
neither = not this and not that
both of you; either of them; neither of them
blocks.narration: Three words for talking about two things. Both, with a plural noun and verb: both books were written in nineteen eighty-five; both of the pencils were broken; both of you are wrong — and it sits after be or between auxiliary and verb: you are both wrong; you must both be more careful. Either means this or the other: there are two methods; either method will give results; either of them works. Neither means not this and not the other: these are incorrect answers; neither is correct; neither of the answers is correct. Two things, three words — count them carefully.

blocks.heading: Example: Right or Wrong?
blocks.problem: Correct the wrong phrases: How many presents did you get? A lot of!

steps.text: A lot of! — wrong: no noun follows; say A lot!
There isn't no time — wrong: isn't any time / there's no time
It's too much loud! — wrong: too loud
My broadband isn't enough fast — wrong: fast enough
How much fruit do we have? None.

blocks.result: A lot; any or no time; too loud; fast enough; None
blocks.narration: Activity two: are the highlighted phrases right or wrong? Correct the wrong ones. How many presents did you get? A lot of — wrong: a lot of must be followed by a noun; in short answers say simply a lot. There isn't no time — wrong, a double negative is impossible: say there isn't any time, or there's no time. It's too much loud — wrong: too much never sits before an adjective; it's too loud. My broadband isn't enough fast — wrong again: enough comes after the adjective, fast enough. And the short-answer trap: how much fruit do we have? Any — no; the correct zero answer is none. Two correct ones: fewer e-books, fewer with countables; plenty of money, more than enough.

items: much / little + uncountable nouns
many / few + countable plurals
a little, a few = some; little, few = almost none
too + adjective; enough after the adjective
Zero: any + not, or no + affirmative verb
blocks.narration: Quantifiers, compressed. Much and little serve uncountable nouns; many and few serve countable plurals. With a — a little, a few — the meaning is some; without a it is almost none. Too pairs with adjectives, never too much big. Enough follows the adjective but comes before a noun. And zero quantity has two grammatical shapes — any with a negative verb, no with an affirmative verb, and none standing alone in short answers. Count first; everything else follows.

blocks.title: The Language of Numbers
blocks.subtitle: Week 3: proportions, averages, figures
blocks.narration: Chapter six: week three's second face, the language of numbers. The lecture builds the numeracy vocabulary you need to work with figures: types of numbers, proportions like majority and minority, and the mean. Engineers, this is your home ground — but in English, and Test One checks every word.

blocks.heading: Types of Numbers
bullets: Prime: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11 (next after 19: 23)
Approximate: roughly correct, not precise
Discrete unit; aggregate = total; random
blocks.narration: First, the vocabulary of number types. A series or set is a group of numbers: one, three, five, seven — the odd numbers; two, four, six, eight — the even numbers. Prime numbers divide only by themselves and one: two, three, five, seven, eleven — so the next prime after nineteen is twenty-three. An approximate number is roughly correct but not precise — estimate first, then check with a calculator. A discrete unit is separate and indivisible. An aggregate is a number reached by totaling a set. And a random number is chosen by chance — you cannot predict it.

blocks.heading: Talking about Proportions
bullets: the majority (56%) of those questioned
the highest percentage / proportion
only two per cent of the population
a small minority; a small fraction
blocks.narration: Academic texts describe parts of a whole with a few phrases. For large parts: the majority — the study found the majority, fifty-six percent, of those questioned were non-smokers; the highest percentage of smokers was found in Naples — or the highest proportion. For small parts: only two per cent of the US population; this small fraction of the population; a small minority of US workers, around five percent. And the usage note: per cent goes after a number — five per cent of the population; inflation rose by two per cent — while percentage and proportion talk more generally: a high proportion of patients; a small proportion of spending.

blocks.heading: The Mean — the Common Average
bullets: Average = a typical value for the data
mean = total of all values / number of values
Sample mean estimates the population mean
Marks 6+8+9+5+6+7: mean about 6.8
blocks.narration: When people talk about averages, they are usually talking about the mean. The idea: one typical value for the whole set of data. The recipe: calculate the total of all the data values, then divide by the number of data values. If your data is a sample, the sample mean estimates the population mean — that is why averages matter. Quick run with the guide's marks: six, eight, nine, five, six, seven. The aggregate — the total — is forty-one. Divide by six values: the mean is about six point eight. Total, divide, done.

blocks.heading: Example: The Maths Tutor's Email
blocks.problem: Complete the email: Don't forget to show your ___. It is a good idea to show how you ___ at your ___.

steps.text: show your workings — all the calculations
how you arrived at your figures
answers hardly even in the right area
distinguish all your calculations
plot the values; take all variables into account

blocks.result: workings; arrived at; figures; area; values; variables
blocks.narration: One of the nicest Week Three tasks is an email from a maths tutor before an exam, rehearsing the number vocabulary in context. Don't forget to show your workings: all the calculations leading up to an answer. It is a good idea to show how you arrived at your figures — in English you arrive at a figure, never reach it; that is why the box word reached stays unused. You would be amazed how many answers are hardly even in the right area — approximately correct. We must be able to distinguish all your calculations. When doing graphs, plot the values carefully. And when you describe an experiment, take all variables into account.

items: Odd, even, prime; approximate vs exact
calculate, estimate, round up/down, tally
majority / high proportion = large
minority / small fraction = small
mean = total divided by the count
blocks.narration: The language of numbers in five lines. Know your types: odd, even, prime, approximate, discrete, aggregate, random. Know your verbs: calculate, estimate, round up and down, total, deduct — and figures tally when they match. Proportions: majority and high proportion mean large; minority, fraction and small percentage mean small. And the mean is the total divided by the number of values. Show your workings in the exam.

blocks.title: Movement, Prepositions and Trends
blocks.subtitle: Week 4: describing movement and change
blocks.narration: Chapter seven: week four turns to reading and writing about movement and change. The grammar focus is prepositions — of movement, of place and time, and the dependent prepositions glued to verbs. The readings describe the speed of change, so we also collect the language of trends. This chapter closes with the format of Test One.

blocks.heading: Prepositions of Movement
rows: The milk passes to the plant.
The storm moves towards the coast.
Pour 50 cc into the test tube.
Put the bottle onto the shelf.
side to side, inside a space
side to side, on a surface
blocks.narration: The Week Four grammar catalogue opens with prepositions of movement. To — movement to a destination: the milk passes to the bottling plant. Into — to the inside of something: pour fifty cubic centimeters of water into the test tube. Onto — to a surface: put the bottle onto the shelf. Through — from one side to the other, inside a space: light does not need to travel through a medium. Across — from one side to the other, on a surface: waves move across the stadium. And towards points a direction without promising arrival: the storm is moving towards the coast. The panel also lists along a line, past a point, up and down, and away from a starting point.

blocks.heading: Prepositions of Place and Time
bullets: at a point: at the bus stop; at 5.30
in an area: in Tashkent, in the bowl
on a surface: on the side of the bottle
on Tuesday; in winter, in the 1960s
blocks.narration: The review cluster puts place and time together. At a point: at the bus stop, and at five thirty for clock times. In an enclosed space: in Tashkent, in the bowl — and for long periods: in winter, in the nineteen sixties. On a surface: on the side of the bottle — and for days and dates: on Tuesday, on Fridays. Two habits carry over from the article chapter: zero article after at, to and from with home, work, school and church; and no article before next and last — see you next week.

blocks.heading: Dependent Prepositions
bullets: depend on; based on; in charge of
arrive at a figure; tally with; divide by
result in; lead to; cope with
be used for measuring (-ing)
blocks.narration: Some prepositions are glued to their verbs and nouns — learn them as whole chunks. Depend on — it all depends on the results. Based on — generalizations are based on facts. Arrive at — a figure or an answer. Tally with — my figures tally with yours. Divide by — divide the total by six. Result in — stereotyping can result in prejudice. Lead to — research leads to discoveries. Cope with — the speed of change is hard to cope with. Be used for plus the -ing form — a thermometer is used for measuring temperature. In charge of — she runs that project. Chunks, not loose words.

blocks.heading: Trend Verbs — the Word Bank
bullets: Up: rise, increase, climb, rocket, double
Top: peak, reach a high, top out
Down: fall, drop, slump, plummet, halve
Flat: level off; Mixed: fluctuate, vary
blocks.narration: The trends worksheet gives a full word bank for graphs. Upward: rise, increase, grow, go up, climb, rocket, take off, double, jump. The highest point: peak, reach a high point, top out. Downward: fall, drop, decrease, decline, go down, slump, plummet, halve. The lowest point: bottom out, hit a low. Stability: remain steady, level off, stabilize, stay the same, hold steady. Fluctuation: fluctuate, vary, go up and down, be volatile. And the tip: if you describe many trends, use a wide variety of vocabulary and be dramatic — sales rocketed tells your audience more than sales increased.

blocks.heading: Example: Describing Market Share
blocks.problem: Complete the extract: Brand A's market share s___ from 9% to 8%; Brand B's share p___ from 6% to just 1%; Brand Z r___ from 10% to 25%.

steps.text: 9% to 8% — a small fall: slipped
6% to just 1% — a dramatic fall: plummeted
10% to 25% — a dramatic rise: rocketed
250,000 to 500,000 euros: doubled
The print budget remained steady.

blocks.result: slipped; plummeted; rocketed; doubled; remained steady
blocks.narration: Now we sit in a results presentation, filling gaps with trend verbs. Brand A's market share slipped from nine percent to eight percent — a small fall, so a small verb. Brand B's share plummeted from six percent to just one — a dramatic crash needs a dramatic verb. Our Brand Z rocketed from ten percent to twenty-five percent. Look at the advertising budget: Brand Z doubled it from two hundred fifty thousand euros to five hundred thousand. The print advertising budget remained steady during the same period. The numbers choose the verb: the distance of the change decides. Other extracts reuse the bank: sales took off over Christmas; Product B slumped below target.

blocks.heading: Example: The Power of Numbers
blocks.problem: Reading: Why did the king have to give the pilgrim so much rice? What is Moore's Law?

steps.text: 1 grain on square 1, doubled on every square
By square 64: more than 18 quintillion grains
Moore's Law: chip power doubles every 18 months
Chain: because of, this has created, as a result
leads to, as a consequence — memorize all four

blocks.result: Doubling adds up fast — and so does change
blocks.narration: Finally, the week four reading: The Power of Numbers. An Indian legend: a king challenges a pilgrim to chess and loses. The price: one grain of rice on the first square, then double on every square after that. By square sixty-four the amount comes to more than eighteen quintillion grains. Its modern twin is Moore's Law: chip power doubles every eighteen months. The reading is one long cause-and-effect chain — learn its connectors. Because of the increase in university students, more people do research; this has created greater competition; as a result, more pressure to publish; new research leads to new discoveries; as a consequence, new technologies arrive more rapidly. Four connectors to memorize: because of, as a result, lead to, as a consequence.

items: to = arrival; towards = direction only
through = 3-D; across = 2-D surface
at a point, in an area, on a surface
Trends: rocket, plummet, fluctuate, level off
Cause: because of, as a result, lead to
blocks.narration: Week four, compressed. Movement: to promises arrival, towards only points; through is three-dimensional, across is two-dimensional. Place and time: at a point or clock time, in an area or long period, on a surface or day. Trends: dramatic verbs beat plain ones, and fluctuate describes ups and downs. Cause and effect: because of, as a result, lead to, as a consequence. Test One covers weeks one to three — our checklists are your revision plan.

items: Routine, permanent = simple; now = continuous
Stative verbs stay simple even for now
First mention a/an; known the; general zero
Quantifiers: countable or uncountable first
Write full sentences; justify every choice
blocks.narration: All four weeks in one revision card. Tense: routine, permanent or general — present simple; now, temporary or changing — present continuous; stative verbs stay simple even now. Articles: first mention or class — a or an; known, unique or superlative — the; general plural or uncountable — no article. Quantifiers: countable or uncountable first, then much or many, little or few, and enough after the adjective. Numbers: majority and high proportion mean large; minority and small fraction mean small; the mean is total divided by count. Write full sentences, justify every choice, and keep five minutes to check verbs and articles.

blocks.narration: And that is the complete guide: every rule, every question form and every answer pattern from weeks one to four of English for Engineering One. You have the present simple, the tense contrast, the article system, the quantifiers, the language of numbers, and the prepositions of movement and change. Review your recap cards, trust the checklists, and walk into Test One with confidence — you are ready. Good luck.
